symptoms: Diamond-shaped or spindle-shaped spots with grey centers and dark borders
Spots may enlarge and merge causing large dead areas
Leaf tips and margins may die back
Seedlings may collapse at infected joints (node blast)
Neck blast: panicle base turns brown-black and breaks
cause: Fungus Magnaporthe oryzae (syn. Pyricularia oryzae). Most destructive rice disease worldwide. Spread by wind-borne conidia. Favored by high nitrogen, prolonged leaf wetness, and temperatures 22-28°C.
treatment: Spray at tillering stage and again at panicle emergence
Reduce nitrogen application if blast appears
prevention: Use resistant varieties: Pusa Basmati-1, PR-114, PR-126
Balanced nitrogen — split nitrogen application
Silicon application (rice husk ash) strengthens cell walls
Remove and destroy straw and stubble
Seed treatment with Tricyclazole or Carbendazim

recommended_pesticide.name: Tricyclazole 75% WP
recommended_pesticide.dosage: 0.6 grams per litre of water (300g per acre)

symptoms: Oval to circular brown spots on leaves, 5-14mm diameter
Spots have grey or white centers with brown borders
Spots may appear on leaf sheaths and panicle branches
Affected grains show brown-black discoloration
Often associated with nutrient-deficient soils
cause: Fungus Bipolaris oryzae (syn. Helminthosporium oryzae). Was the primary cause of the 1943 Bengal Famine. Seed-borne and soil-borne. Thrives in nutrient-deficient soils, especially potassium and silicon deficiency.
prevention: Soil testing and balanced fertilization
Use healthy, certified seed
Seed treatment with Carbendazim 50% WP at 2g/kg seed
Apply potassium and zinc as per soil test recommendations
Maintain proper water management

symptoms: Water-soaked lesions along leaf margins that turn yellow then white
Lesions extend along veins, giving leaves a 'scorched' appearance
Yellowish bacterial ooze visible on cut leaf edges in early morning
Severely infected leaves dry up from margins
Whole plant may wilt and die in kresek phase (seedlings)
cause: Bacterium Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae. Enters through wounds and stomata. Spread by rain splash, wind, and contaminated irrigation water. Favored by high nitrogen, storms, and temperatures 28-34°C.
treatment: Apply Streptocycline at 0.5g + Copper Oxychloride at 2.5g per litre
Avoid field operations when leaves are wet
prevention: Use BLB-resistant varieties: PR-114, Pusa-44 (some resistance)
Balanced nitrogen — avoid excess urea
Proper field drainage
Avoid clipping seedling tips during transplanting
Avoid movement between wet fields

symptoms: Oval to irregular greenish-grey lesions on leaf sheaths near water line
Lesions have dark brown borders
Lesions move upward affecting successive sheaths and leaves
White mycelium may be visible on affected sheaths
Sclerotia (small brown-white bodies) form on sheaths
cause: Fungus Rhizoctonia solani. Soil-borne — sclerotia survive in soil for years. Spread through sclerotia floating in irrigation water. Favored by high nitrogen, dense planting, high humidity, and temperatures 28-32°C.
treatment: Spray targeting the lower leaf sheath area
Reduce water level to expose lower sheaths
prevention: Maintain proper plant spacing — wider spacing reduces spread
Balanced nitrogen — split applications
Avoid continuous flooding
Deep ploughing in summer to bury sclerotia
Remove and destroy infected stubble
